source.title: LLM Misalignment via Adversarial RLHF Platforms

record.file_problem: none; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: Tests a related safety-misalignment outcome in an RLHF setting: it poisons preference labels and evaluates generated-response rewards, rather than testing the specified refusal, token-position, or bypass claims.
record.gate_note: The study reports shifts in clean-reward-model scores after PPO fine-tuning with poisoned preference data. These scores do not measure refusal or harmful-completion rates, so the findings are recorded as related but not as evidence for any listed version. The reward-model accuracy results in Table 1 assess reward-model performance, not the listed behavioral outcomes.
record.test_reason: The study does not test any version. It deliberately corrupts RLHF by flipping hate-speech preference labels, then PPO-trains base GPT-2 models (117M–762M), which were never safety-trained. Its only behavioural measure is the distribution of clean-reward-model scores, shown as figures. It reports no harmful-compliance or refusal rate, no per-token analysis, no bypass test, no localization and no deepening method. It cites Qi et al. (2310.03693) only in related work. The record's 'tests/T3' should be cites_only/T6.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate. The authors conclude that an adversarial RLHF platform flipping labels on targeted preference samples corrupts the reward model and misaligns the RLHF-tuned LLM in the targeted domain. They add that the effect depends heavily on the dataset and the samples affected.
record.recipe_differences: The study manipulates preference-pair labels and performs PPO fine-tuning; it does not use the original supervised fine-tuning method or token-depth measurements.
record.method_sensitivity: The paper reports that results depend on dataset and affected samples; its text also notes that fully attacked reward models produce significant distribution changes and that the large model's response-quality shift differs from the others.

fits_no_version.finding: Targeted label-flipping on hate-speech preference pairs (25–100% of targeted samples) shifts the clean-RM score distribution of PPO-trained GPT-2 outputs, mostly toward lower rewards. The results are shown only as histograms.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Targeted preference-label poisoning during RLHF yields reward-model-judged misalignment in the targeted domain.

record.problems: Experiments use models with fewer than 1 billion parameters and no extensive hyperparameter search. The authors note that a trained reward model may not capture all human preferences and that large-scale human evaluation would be more reliable. Behavioral evidence is presented as reward-distribution plots rather than direct harmful-completion or refusal rates.
record.rows_left_out: No qualifying results omitted. Table 1 reward-model accuracy results are not included because they measure reward-model accuracy, not generated-model safety behavior.

untested.parts: No harmful-example fine-tuning of a safety-trained model. Attacked models start from base GPT-2, not from an aligned model. No harmful-compliance rate is reported.
No per-token KL between aligned and base models.
No prefilling, suffix or decoding attacks.
No localization of safety to weights or ranks.
No analysis of why alignment is shallow.
No deepening method is trained or evaluated.

record.verdict_notes: All 24 rows are correctly linked to none and marked cannot_determine: they are figure-only reward-score distributions, not rates of harmful compliance. The subjects are base GPT-2 models trained by RLHF from scratch with a poisoned reward model, so even V1's setting (a safety-trained model) does not apply. Table 1 reward-model accuracies (e.g., DistilBERT 65.74 clean vs 59.08 at 100%) are correctly excluded as reward-model performance, not model behaviour.

versions.untested_parts: Does not test ordinary harmful-example fine-tuning on a safety-trained chat model or measure harmful-request compliance/refusal.
Does not test ordinary or carefully chosen benign fine-tuning.
Does not measure per-token KL divergence or compare aligned and base models across response positions.
Does not test compliant prefills, adversarial suffixes, or decoding changes.
Does not localize safety behavior to weights or ranks.
Does not investigate why safety behavior would be shallow.
Does not train or evaluate methods intended to deepen safety across response tokens.
